# Hypercalcemia

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Nephrology > Fluids, electrolytes, and acid-base disorders > Hypercalcemia*

[Original Article Link](/library/UI0bXh)

---

## Summary

Hypercalcemia refers to high serum <u>calcium</u> levels (total Ca > 10.5 mg/dL or ionized <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> > 5.25 mg/dL). The most common <u>causes of hypercalcemia</u> are <u>primary hyperparathyroidism</u> and <u>malignancy</u> involving paraneoplastic production of <u>parathyroid hormone-related protein</u> (<u>PTHrP</u>). Manifestations of hypercalcemia include <u>nephrolithiasis</u>, bone <u>pain</u>, abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>polyuria</u>, <u>muscle weakness</u>, and neuropsychiatric symptoms. The most important initial diagnostic steps are ruling out <u>factitious hypercalcemia</u> (by measuring <u>ionized calcium</u> or calculating the <u>corrected calcium</u>) and measuring intact <u>PTH</u> levels (to differentiate between <u>PTH-mediated hypercalcemia</u> and <u>non-PTH-mediated hypercalcemia</u>). Management depends on the severity of the <u>calcium imbalance</u>. Mild and asymptomatic <u>moderate hypercalcemia</u> is treated with oral rehydration and low <u>calcium</u> intake, while symptomatic or <u>severe hypercalcemia</u> is a potentially life-threatening <u>medical emergency</u> requiring hospitalization and immediate treatment with IV fluid repletion and medications that inhibit bone resorption (e.g., <u>calcitonin</u>, <u>bisphosphonates</u>). In addition, identification and treatment of the underlying cause of hypercalcemia are essential.




See “<u>Hypocalcemia</u>” for details on <u>calcium</u> physiology and <u>homeostasis</u>.

---

## Definitions

* Hypercalcemia is a <u>total serum calcium</u> concentration of > 10.5 mg/dL or ionized (free) <u>calcium</u> concentration of > 5.25 mg/dL. [[1]](/library/RAYlj7)

* True hypercalcemia: ↑ <u>ionized calcium</u> or ↑ <u>corrected calcium</u> (regardless of <u>total calcium</u> level); can be symptomatic.

* Factitious hypercalcemia: ↑ <u>total calcium</u> with normal ionized (non-protein bound, physiologically active) <u>calcium</u> or normal <u>corrected calcium</u> level; asymptomatic.
* The increase in <u>total serum calcium</u> levels is caused by increased protein levels, for example:

* Hyperalbuminemia in <u>dehydrated</u> patients

* Paraproteinemia in patients with <u>multiple myeloma</u>.

---

## Etiology

Hypercalcemia may be due to <u>PTH</u>-mediated or non-<u>PTH</u>-mediated causes. <u>Primary hyperparathyroidism</u> and <u>malignancy</u> are the most common causes, accounting for ∼ 90% of all cases.  [[2]](/library/VKYG2J)




| <br><u>Causes of hypercalcemia</u> [[2]](/library/VKYG2J)[[3]](/library/RFbl3v)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Types of hypercalcemia | Etiology | Pathophysiology |
| PTH-mediated hypercalcemia | <u>Primary hyperparathyroidism</u> | <br><br>* <u>Parathyroid adenoma</u> or <u>hyperplasia</u> (sporadic or in <u>multiple endocrine neoplasias</u>)<br><br>* Excess <u>PTH</u> → ↑ production of <u>1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D</u> via stimulation of <u>1-alpha-hydroxylase</u> synthesis in the <u>kidneys</u><br><br>* Usually asymptomatic  [[2]](/library/VKYG2J)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Tertiary hyperparathyroidism</u> | <br><br>* <u>Renal failure</u> → chronic <u>secondary hyperparathyroidism</u> → autonomous activation of one or more <u>parathyroid gland</u><br><br>* Usually seen in patients with <u>ESRD</u>  [[4]](/library/bubHpv)<br><br><br> |  |
| <u>Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia</u> | <br>* See “Familial hypocalcuric hypercalcemia” in “Subtypes and variants.”<br><br> |  |
| Medications | <br>* <u>Lithium</u> reduces renal <u>calcium</u> excretion and alters the <u>PTH</u> secretion set point  [[5]](/library/gHbFpE)[[6]](/library/wXWhZ40)<br><br> |  |
| Non-PTH-mediated hypercalcemia | Hypercalcemia of malignancy | <br><br>* Most common cause: paraneoplastic production of <u>PTHrP</u>  (e.g., <u>squamous cell carcinomas</u> of the <u>lung</u>, head, and neck; <u>breast</u>, ovarian, <u>bladder</u>, and <u>renal cancer</u>; <u>lymphoma</u> and <u>leukemia</u>)<br><br>* <u>Osteolytic metastases</u> (e.g., <u>multiple myeloma</u>, <u>breast cancer</u>, <u>lymphoma</u> and <u>leukemia</u>, <u>renal cancer</u>)<br><br>* Paraneoplastic production of <u>1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D</u>: e.g., <u>lymphoma</u>, <u>ovarian dysgerminoma</u><br><br>* Typically manifests acutely with severe symptoms and signs  [[7]](/library/fHbkpE)<br><br><br> |
| Granulomatous disorders (e.g., <u>sarcoidosis</u>) | <br>* Hydroxylase activity in activated <u>mononuclear cells</u> produces <u>1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D</u> outside of the <u>kidneys</u>.<br><br> |  |
| Medications | <br><br>* <u>Thiazide diuretics</u> reduce renal <u>calcium</u> excretion.  [[8]](/library/IgXY9x)<br><br>* Excess <u>vitamin D</u> increases intestinal <u>calcium</u> absorption.<br><br>* <u>Calcium</u> supplements and <u>antacids</u><br><br>* <u>Vitamin A</u> and <u>vitamin A</u> derivatives (e.g., <u>isotretinoin</u>) directly stimulate bone resorption. [[9]](/library/ogX0wx)<br><br><br> |  |
| <u>Thyrotoxicosis</u> | <br>* ↑ <u>Thyroid hormone</u> → ↑ <u>osteoclastic</u> activity → ↑ bone resorption<br><br> |  |
| Long periods of <u>immobilization</u> | <br><br>* Lack of <u>weight-bearing</u> activities → <u>osteoclast</u> activation → bone demineralization → hypercalcemia<br><br>* Usually occurs in patients with high <u>bone turnover</u> at baseline  [[5]](/library/gHbFpE)<br><br><br> |  |
| Milk-alkali syndrome | <br><br>* Consumption of large amounts of <u>calcium carbonate</u><br><br>* Presents with hypercalcemia, <u>metabolic alkalosis</u>, and <u>acute kidney injury</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <u>Adrenal insufficiency</u> | <br>* The exact pathophysiology is unknown; several mechanisms have been proposed. [[10]](/library/voYAdJ)<br><br>* <u>Hypovolemia</u> → ↓ <u>GFR</u> → ↓ <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> excretion → ↑ blood concentration of <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u><br><br>* ↑ <u>1α-hydroxylase</u> → ↑ <u>calcitriol</u> → ↑ <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> intestinal absorption<br><br>* ↓ Stanniocalcin<br><br> |  |

> For <u>causes of hypercalcemia</u>, remember “Thinking Chimpanzees!”
> Thinking: <u>Thiazides</u>, <u>thyroid</u>
> Calcium supplementation
> Hyperparathyroidism
> Immobilization, inherited (<u>FHH</u>)
> Milk-alkali synd., meds (<u>thiazides</u>, <u>lithium</u>)
> Paraneoplastic <u>PTHrP</u>
> Adrenal insufficiency
> Neoplasm (<u>multiple myeloma</u>, <u>breast</u>, <u>lung</u>)
> Zollinger-Ellison syndrome

> [!TIP]
> Severe/symptomatic hypercalcemia usually develops acutely and is typically caused by excessive <u>osteoclast</u>-mediated bone resorption, most commonly in association with <u>malignancy</u>.




> [!TIP]
> In <u>primary hyperparathyroidism</u>, serum <u>calcium</u> is typically lower and rises more slowly than in <u>hypercalcemia of malignancy</u>. Patients are, therefore, less symptomatic.

---

## Clinical features

The clinical presentation is variable and ranges from asymptomatic presentation in <u>mild hypercalcemia</u> to life-threatening clinical features in <u>severe hypercalcemia</u>. See “<u>Classification of hypercalcemia</u>.” [[6]](/library/wXWhZ40)[[11]](/library/kIYm1q)




* <u>Nephrolithiasis</u>, <u>nephrocalcinosis</u> (<u>calcium</u> oxalate > <u>calcium phosphate stones</u>)

* Bone <u>pain</u>, <u>arthralgias</u>, <u>myalgias</u>, <u>fractures</u>

* <u>Constipation</u>

* Abdominal <u>pain</u>

* <u>Nausea and vomiting</u>

* <u>Anorexia</u>

* <u>Peptic ulcer disease</u>  [[12]](/library/BoYzVJ)

* <u>Pancreatitis</u>

* Neuropsychiatric symptoms such as <u>anxiety</u>, <u>depression</u>, fatigue, and cognitive dysfunction

* <u>Somnolence</u>

* <u>Obtundation</u> and <u>coma</u> indicate progression to <u>hypercalcemic crisis</u>

* Diminished muscle excitability

* Cardiac <u>arrhythmias</u>

* <u>Muscle weakness</u>, <u>paresis</u>

* <u>Polyuria</u> and <u>dehydration</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Hypercalcemia can cause <u>pancreatitis</u>. <u>Hypocalcemia</u> in patients with <u>pancreatitis</u> suggests <u>pancreatic</u> <u>necrosis</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> The presentation of hypercalcemia includes stones (<u>nephrolithiasis</u>), bones (bone <u>pain</u>, <u>arthralgias</u>), thrones (increased <u>urinary frequency</u>), groans (abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>), and psychiatric overtones (<u>anxiety</u>, <u>depression</u>, fatigue). Note that these are also the findings of <u>vitamin D</u> overdose!




> [!TIP]
> Acute hypercalcemia is more likely to present with symptoms, whereas hypercalcemia that has progressed over time is more likely to be asymptomatic.

## Classification

<u>Laboratory values</u> and the presence of symptoms should be used in conjunction to determine the need for treatment. Acutely symptomatic <u>moderate hypercalcemia</u> and <u>severe hypercalcemia</u> are <u>medical emergencies</u> and require hospital admission and immediate initiation of treatment.




* Mild hypercalcemia

* <u>Total calcium</u> 10.5–12 mg/dL

* OR <u>ionized calcium</u> 5.25–8 mg/dL

* Typically asymptomatic

* Moderate hypercalcemia

* <u>Total calcium</u> 12–14 mg/dL

* OR <u>ionized calcium</u> 8–10 mg/dL

* Can be asymptomatic or symptomatic (especially if it develops acutely)

* Severe hypercalcemia, also known as <u>hypercalcemic crisis</u>

* <u>Total calcium</u> > 14 mg/dL

* OR <u>ionized calcium</u> > 10 mg/dL

* A life-threatening condition that can be associated with:

* <u>Dehydration</u> (due to <u>ADH</u> resistance and <u>vomiting</u>)

* <u>Oliguria</u>/<u>anuria</u>

* Altered consciousness

* <u>Psychosis</u>

---

## Subtypes and variants

### Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (<u>FHH</u>) [[13]](/library/vXWA-P0)




* Etiology: : <u>autosomal dominant</u> <u>inactivating mutation</u> in the <u>CaSR</u> <u>gene</u> → decreased <u>sensitivity</u> of G-coupled calcium-sensing receptors in <u>parathyroid glands</u> and <u>kidneys</u>;  → higher levels of <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> required to suppress <u>PTH</u> and higher reabsorption of <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> in the <u>kidney</u> → hypocalciuria with <u>mild hypercalcemia</u> and normal or increased <u>PTH</u> levels

* Clinical features

* Usually asymptomatic (incidental finding)

* <u>Neonatal hypocalcemia</u> in children of mothers with <u>FHH</u> (e.g., <u>paresthesias</u>, muscle spasms, <u>seizures</u>)  [[14]](/library/h1Wcg40)

* Diagnosis

* Hypercalcemia and inappropriately normal or increased <u>PTH</u>

* Hypocalciuria

* ↓ 24-hour <u>urinary calcium excretion</u> (< 200 mg/24 h) [[15]](/library/31WSg40)

* ↓ <u>Urine Ca/Cr clearance ratio</u> (< 0.02)

* See also “<u>Assessment of urinary calcium excretion</u>.”

* Confirmatory <u>genetic testing</u> for <u>CaSR</u> <u>gene mutations</u>

* Therapy

* No treatment necessary

* <u>Cinacalcet</u> may be considered in patients with symptomatic <u>FHH</u>  [[16]](/library/sZct1a0)

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[1]](/library/RAYlj7)[[2]](/library/VKYG2J)[[3]](/library/RFbl3v)[[5]](/library/gHbFpE)[[6]](/library/wXWhZ40)




* Confirm true hypercalcemia: measure <u>ionized calcium</u> OR calculate <u>corrected calcium</u> using <u>total calcium</u> and serum <u>albumin</u>.

* Risk assessment and <u>global</u> evaluation

* Determine severity: see “<u>Classification of hypercalcemia</u>”

* Begin treatment immediately for patients with <u>severe hypercalcemia</u> or symptomatic patients while pursuing further diagnostic workup.

* Perform <u>volume status assessment</u>.

* Obtain <u>ECG</u>

* Identify concurrent <u>electrolyte</u> abnormalities.

* Initial evaluation of underlying etiology

* Measure serum intact <u>PTH</u>: initial study to determine the <u>etiology of hypercalcemia</u> and to differentiate <u>PTH-mediated hypercalcemia</u> from <u>non-PTH-mediated hypercalcemia</u>

* Order other routine tests as guided by clinician suspicion : e.g. <u>alkaline phosphatase</u>, <u>TSH</u>

* Intermediate evaluation of underlying etiology: Consider these studies based on the results of initial evaluation.

* Normal or ↑ <u>PTH</u>: urine <u>calcium</u> excretion

* ↓ <u>PTH</u>: <u>PTHrP</u> and <u>vitamin D</u> levels  [[2]](/library/VKYG2J)[[17]](/library/08beOv)

* Advanced evaluation of underlying etiology: Consider these studies based on combined results of the initial and intermediate evaluations (see “Other evaluation to consider” for details).[[1]](/library/RAYlj7)[[5]](/library/gHbFpE)

* ↑ <u>PTHrP</u> or ↑ <u>1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D</u>: investigations for tumors, <u>lymphoma</u>, or <u>granulomatous diseases</u>

* Normal <u>PTHrP</u> and normal or ↓ <u>vitamin D</u> levels: investigations for <u>multiple myeloma</u>, <u>thyrotoxicosis</u>, Paget disease, <u>vitamin A toxicity</u>, or <u>adrenal insufficiency</u>

* ↓ Urine <u>calcium</u> excretion: investigations for <u>FHH</u> (e.g., <u>genetic testing</u>, see <u>FHH</u>)

* Adjunctive studies: consider on an individual basis (e.g., <u>bone densitometry</u> or detailed <u>laboratory evaluation of bone disease</u>)





![Diagnosis of hypercalcemia](media/isifpth11xzh4k5n3rz3p439.jpg)

Diagnosis of hypercalcemia




> [!WARNING]
> Severe or symptomatic hypercalcemia is a <u>medical emergency</u>. Treatment should be initiated immediately, in parallel with diagnostic workup.




### Routine evaluation [[2]](/library/VKYG2J)[[5]](/library/gHbFpE)




* Serum <u>calcium</u>

* <u>Total calcium</u>

* <u>Ionized calcium</u>

* Corrected calcium (mg/dL) = measured total <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> (mg/dL) + [0.8 x (4 - <u>albumin</u> concentration in g/dL)]

* Other <u>laboratory studies</u>

* <u>Albumin</u>

* <u>Phosphate</u>: typically low in <u>primary hyperparathyroidism</u> and <u>PTHrP</u>-mediated hypercalcemia  [[5]](/library/gHbFpE)

* <u>BMP</u>

* <u>Alkaline phosphatase</u>

* <u>ABG</u>/<u>VBG</u>

* <u>CBC</u>

* <u>ECG</u> findings may include:

* <u>QT interval shortening</u> and in <u>severe hypercalcemia</u> <u>J wave</u>

* <u>Bradycardia</u>

* <u>Arrhythmias</u>





> [!TIP]
> The <u>corrected calcium</u> concentration, calculated using serum <u>albumin</u>, may not be accurate in the setting of major acid-base imbalances. In patients with significant <u>alkalemia</u> or <u>acidemia</u>, it is recommended to measure <u>ionized calcium</u> directly.




![Calcium correction for hypoalbuminemia](media/pqd5s6w9f42eo43ct2ytqblm.jpg)

Calcium correction for hypoalbuminemia




### Evaluation to determine underlying etiology




* Serum intact <u>PTH</u>

* Normal or ↑ <u>PTH</u>: <u>PTH-mediated hypercalcemia</u>

* ↓ <u>PTH</u>: <u>non-PTH-mediated hypercalcemia</u>

* PTHrP

* A protein produced by malignant cells that has the same function as <u>parathyroid hormone</u>.

* Production of <u>PTHrP</u> is the most common cause of <u>hypercalcemia of malignancy</u>.

* ↑ <u>PTHrP</u>: solid <u>malignancy</u>  or <u>neuroendocrine tumors</u>

* Normal or ↓ <u>PTHrP</u>: Consider other causes of non-<u>PTH</u>-mediated hypercalcemia (see “<u>Etiology of hypercalcemia</u>”).

* <u>Vitamin D</u> levels

* ↑ <u>1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D</u>: <u>lymphoma</u>, granulomatous disease, or <u>calcitriol</u> ingestion

* ↑ <u>25-hydroxyvitamin D</u>: <u>vitamin D intoxication</u> (i.e., due to ingestion of <u>ergocalciferol</u>, <u>cholecalciferol</u>, or <u>calcidiol</u>)

* Assessment of urinary calcium excretion [[2]](/library/VKYG2J)[[5]](/library/gHbFpE)[[18]](/library/Yubnpv)[[19]](/library/78b4Lv)

* Studies 

* 24-hour urinary excretion of <u>calcium</u>

* AND/OR urine Ca/Cr clearance ratio (an index of renal <u>calcium</u> excretion; determined by measuring the concentrations of <u>calcium</u> and <u>creatinine</u> in the serum and in a <u>24-hour urine collection</u> sample)  [[20]](/library/-FbDkv)

* Interpretation [[5]](/library/gHbFpE)[[19]](/library/78b4Lv)

* Normal or ↑ urine <u>calcium</u> (<u>urine Ca/Cr clearance ratio</u> > 0.02 or 24-hour urine <u>calcium</u> > 200 mg/24 hmg): <u>primary hyperparathyroidism</u> > 100 mg/24 h [[18]](/library/Yubnpv)

* ↓ Urine <u>calcium</u> (<u>urine Ca/Cr clearance ratio</u> < 0.02 or 24-hour urine <u>calcium</u> < 200 mg/24 h): <u>FHH</u> or <u>primary hyperparathyroidism</u>; consider <u>genetic testing</u> for <u>FHH</u>.  [[21]](/library/a8bQOv)





> [!TIP]
> Measurement of serum intact <u>PTH</u> level is the key initial study for confirmed hypercalcemia with no immediately evident etiology.




### Other evaluation to consider [[1]](/library/RAYlj7)[[5]](/library/gHbFpE)




* <u>Laboratory studies</u>

* <u>TSH</u>, T4, T3: assess for <u>thyrotoxicosis</u>

* <u>Cortisol</u> and <u>ACTH stimulation test</u>: assess for <u>adrenal insufficiency</u>

* <u>Vitamin A</u> levels: assess for <u>vitamin A toxicity</u>

* <u>Serum protein electrophoresis</u> and urine <u>Bence Jones protein</u>: assess for <u>multiple myeloma</u>

* Detailed <u>laboratory evaluation of bone disease</u>: further evaluation of bone disorders

* <u>Genetic testing</u>: See <u>FHH</u>.

* Imaging

* CT chest, abdomen, <u>pelvis</u>: assess for tumors, <u>lymphoma</u>, or <u>granulomatous diseases</u>

* <u>Skeletal survey</u>: assess for lytic bone lesions and Paget disease

* <u>Bone densitometry</u>: further evaluation of patients with <u>primary hyperparathyroidism</u> [[17]](/library/08beOv)

---

## Treatment

### Approach [[2]](/library/VKYG2J)[[5]](/library/gHbFpE)




* All patients

* Ensure adequate <u>supportive care</u>.

* Identify and treat the underlying cause (see “<u>Etiology of hypercalcemia</u>”).

* Consider consulting <u>endocrinology</u>, nephrology, oncology, and/or <u>surgery</u> services as needed.

* <u>Severe hypercalcemia</u> and symptomatic <u>moderate hypercalcemia</u>: Admit to hospital and treat as a <u>medical emergency</u>.

* Rapidly lower <u>calcium</u> levels.

* Start <u>IV fluid therapy</u> with <u>0.9% NaCl</u>.

* Consider adding <u>diuretics</u> if there is <u>volume overload</u>.

* Initiate pharmacotherapy: e.g., <u>calcitonin</u>, <u>bisphosphonates</u>, <u>denosumab</u>.

* Consider <u>targeted therapy</u> based on suspected etiology: e.g., <u>surgery</u>, <u>calcimimetics</u>, <u>corticosteroids</u>.

* Treat any complications: e.g., <u>arrhythmias</u>, <u>nephrolithiasis</u>.

* Consider <u>hemodialysis</u> for refractory life-threatening hypercalcemia or if other therapies are contraindicated (e.g., <u>bisphosphonates</u> in severe <u>renal failure</u>).

* <u>Mild hypercalcemia</u> or asymptomatic <u>moderate hypercalcemia</u>: Consider inpatient vs. outpatient therapy on an individual basis.

* Acute treatment other than <u>supportive care</u> and treatment of the underlying cause is usually not necessary.

* Follow <u>calcium</u> levels and monitor for the development of symptoms.  [[2]](/library/VKYG2J)





### <u>Supportive care</u>




* Ensure adequate hydration.

* Reduce dietary intake of <u>calcium</u>.

* Avoid;  potentially aggravating medications (e.g., <u>thiazides</u>, <u>lithium</u>, <u>vitamin D</u>, <u>calcidiol</u>, <u>calcitriol</u>).

* Encourage mobility and avoid prolonged bed rest/inactivity. [[5]](/library/gHbFpE)





### <u>Fluid therapy</u> and <u>volume status</u> management




* IV fluid repletion with <u>0.9% NaCl</u> DOSAGE: typically 4–6 L in 24 hours

* Obtain serial <u>calcium</u> checks and monitor urine output and <u>volume status</u>.

* Consider IV <u>loop diuretic</u> (e.g. IV <u>furosemide</u> DOSAGE) ONLY if there are signs of <u>volume overload</u> (e.g., <u>pulmonary congestion</u>, significant <u>peripheral edema</u>).  [[22]](/library/eEbxuv)





> [!NOTE]
> Thiazide <u>diuretics</u> enhance Tubular <u>calcium</u> upTake: Discontinue them in hypercalcemia. Loop <u>diuretics</u> Lose <u>calcium</u>: They may be used to treat <u>fluid overload</u> in patients with hypercalcemia.




### Standard pharmacotherapy




Pharmacotherapy is aimed at inhibiting bone resorption.




* Consider <u>calcitonin</u> DOSAGE for rapid-onset, short-term control of hypercalcemia. 

* Reduces serum <u>calcium</u> within 2–6 hours, with maximal effect within 12–24 hours

* Often limited by <u>tachyphylaxis</u> after 48 hours of use

* <u>Bisphosphonates</u> for slow-onset, long-term control of hypercalcemia

* Options

* <u>Zoledronic acid</u> DOSAGE  [[3]](/library/RFbl3v)

* Pamidronate DOSAGE

* Typically lead to normalization of serum <u>calcium</u> within 2–4 days, with effect duration of days to weeks following a single dose

* The dose may be repeated, if needed, after a minimum of 7 days.

* Contraindicated in severe <u>CKD</u> (<u>CrCl</u> < 30 mL/min)





### Alternative therapeutic options




These treatment options may be considered if hypercalcemia is resistant to other measures or the use of <u>bisphosphonates</u> is contraindicated due to severe <u>renal failure</u>.




* <u>Denosumab</u> DOSAGE  [[2]](/library/VKYG2J)[[5]](/library/gHbFpE)[[23]](/library/JubsHv)

* <u>Hemodialysis</u> may additionally be considered in the following circumstances:

* Aggressive fluid repletion is contraindicated (e.g., patients with <u>fluid overload</u> due to severe <u>heart failure</u> or <u>oliguric</u> <u>AKI</u>).

* Immediate reduction of <u>calcium</u> levels is necessary due to life-threatening symptomatic hypercalcemia.  [[24]](/library/ROXlHy)





### <u>Targeted therapies</u>




* Hypercalcemia due to primary or <u>tertiary hyperparathyroidism</u> [[4]](/library/bubHpv)[[17]](/library/08beOv)[[25]](/library/H81KLi0)

* Surgical management preferred: partial or total <u>parathyroidectomy</u>

* <u>Calcimimetics</u> (e.g., <u>cinacalcet</u> DOSAGE) for patients unable to undergo <u>surgery</u>

* See “Treatment” in “<u>Hyperparathyroidism</u>.”

* Hypercalcemia due to <u>lymphoma</u>, <u>granulomatous diseases</u>, or <u>vitamin D intoxication</u>: <u>systemic glucocorticoids</u> (e.g., <u>prednisone</u> DOSAGE)  [[3]](/library/RFbl3v)

* <u>Hypercalcemia of malignancy</u> [[26]](/library/EXW8-P0)[[27]](/library/DXW1Z40)

* Monotherapy: <u>Denosumab</u> DOSAGE  is preferred to IV <u>bisphosphonates</u>. [[26]](/library/EXW8-P0)

* Combination therapy for <u>severe hypercalcemia</u>: <u>calcitonin</u> PLUS either <u>denosumab</u> or <u>bisphosphonate</u>

* Hypercalcemia due to parathyroid <u>carcinoma</u> [[26]](/library/EXW8-P0)[[27]](/library/DXW1Z40)

* Initial treatment with one of the following: <u>calcimimetic</u>, IV <u>bisphosphonates</u>, <u>denosumab</u>

* If hypercalcemia is not adequately controlled with either <u>calcimimetic</u> or <u>bisphosphonate</u>/<u>denosumab</u>, consider adding an additional agent.
